newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German H1 bank profits point to good 1997.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German H1 bank profits point to good 1997.

text.p: Dresdner Bank AG, Germany's Number Two bank, on Tuesday reported a 23 percent rise in earnings in the first half of 1997, confirming a trend of rising earnings in a sector awash with merger speculation.
Dresdner said its operating profit rose to over 1.7 billion marks from 1.42 billion in the year earlier, just above analysts' average expectations of a rise to 1.67 billion marks.

Adding further fuel to banking merger speculation but putting early pressure on its share price, Dresdner also said it planned to raise its base capital by 120 million marks by issuing new shares in the ratio one for 20 held.
"With this step, we will in particular broaden our scope for strategic moves," Dresdner said in a statement.
It said it expected the subscription period for the new shares would run from August 14 to August 28, and said the capital raise was subject to supervisory board approval.

Also on Tuesday, Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank AG (Hypo-Bank), Germany's fifth largest bank and soon to be merged with fellow Bavarian bank Bayerische Vereinsbank AG, said operating profit rose 17.2 percent to 651.7 million marks.
The result was slightly below analysts' expectations for an operating profit figure of 686.5 million marks.
The results end a half-year reporting season which has shown the top five banks firmly on course for record earnings in 1997, barring a market meltdown in the latter half.
Deutsche Bank AG, Europe's largest bank, last week beat forecasts by announcing a 27.5 percent rise in net income to 1.5 billion marks in the first half.

Vereinsbank, Germany's Number Four, raised its operating profit by a slightly lower-than-expected 15.2 percent to 765.7 million marks. And Commerzbank's pre-tax profit rose 24.7 percent to 1.65 billion marks.
But investors are paying scant attention to earnings at a time when speculation of further mega-mergers has gripped the banking sector.

Last week's Bavarian merger news, which will transform Germany's banking landscape by creating Germany's second largest bank and Europe's largest property finance group, has sparked heightened speculation on how rivals will respond.
Dresdner's possible role is being particularly closely scrutinised.

While no consensus has emerged on who may link up with whom if at all, some analysts see Dresdner eventually joining forces with the new merged Bavarian bank, Bayerische Hypo- und Vereinsbank AG (BHV).
That would provide BHV with the investment banking base it lacks and giving it a nationwide retail branch network. BHV's branches will be largely confined to southern Germany.
Such a move would probably not be blocked by cartel authorities given the fragmented nature of Germany's banking market. Even Deutsche has a market share of just five percent.
Analysts say any link-up between Dresdner and BHV would probably incorporate Allianz given the sizeable cross-shareholdings among the groups.
Allianz owns roughly 22 percent of Dresdner and will own about 16 percent of BHV while Dresdner holds 10 percent of Allianz.

Some analysts have speculated that Deutsche, Dresdner or a foreign bank may merge with or buy Commerzbank, which has come under added pressure to find an ally either in Germany or abroad in response to the Bavarian move.
Commerzbank last week reaffirmed its determination to remain independent, saying its first-half results showed earnings were strong enough to stay on its own.
